summary.value: This paper studies the effects of DP on hallucination, in the setting where DP is used to protect private information when using RAG in LLMs. The authors construct two RAG benchmarks in the medical and financial domains, with PII annotations. They use the Confidence Gap (CG) to detect hallucination, and they show that hallucinated sentences have lower CG than supported ones, and that sentences containing PII have higher CG. The authors propose PEARL, a differentially private entropy-aware language generation framework, where after producing an initial response with the exponential mechanism, they reallocate the privacy budget at the sentence level and selectively regenerate segments flagged by CG as hallucination-prone or containing PII. They show that PEARL enables privacy while reducing hallucination.

strengths.value:
- This work studies how DP affects hallucination, which is important and under-explored.
- The results show that PEARL performs well compared to the baselines, and that it yields lower PII leakage.
- This paper contributes two RAG benchmarks in the medical and financial domains with PII annotations, which will be useful for future studies.

weaknesses.value:
- The classification of sentences into supported/unsupported/uncertain categories, as well as the labeling of PII, was done by GPT-4o, and it is unclear how accurate these classifications and labels are.
- The datasets are synthetically generated using GPT-4o, and may not be reflective of real data. While the authors mention that they engaged domain experts to check the data, it would be good to give more details on what percentage of the documents were checked, and the methodology for checking.
- The main evaluation was only done on two LLMs. It might be useful to evaluate on a more diverse range of LLMs with different sizes to check that the results generalize.
- PEARL might lead to a higher computational cost and latency.

questions.value:
- Could more details be given on how the datasets are checked to be similar to real data?
- What is the computational overhead and latency of using PEARL?
- How accurate are the classification into categories and PII labeling done by GPT-4o?

We are truly grateful for the reviewer’s thoughtful and constructive feedback. Below, we provide our detailed responses to each comment.

> W1. The classification of sentences into supported/unsupported/uncertain categories, as well as the labeling of PII, was done by GPT-4o, and it is unclear how accurate these classifications and labels are.
>
> Q3. How accurate are the classification into categories and PII labeling done by GPT-4o?

We use LLM-based annotators for hallucination classification and PII extraction, as prior studies have utilized the annotators on these tasks [1,2] given gold references.

To validate the labeling process, we instructed another widely used LLMs, **Claude Sonnet 4.5 model** to annotate hallucinations following the same procedure described in the manuscript. The table presents the number of examples on which GPT-4o and Claude 4.5 agreed or disagreed, broken down by domain. The results show that **the majority of examples are consistent with the GPT-4o annotations.**

|  | Agree | Disagree |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Medical | 3164 (95.64%) | 166 (4.36%) |
| Financial | 1245 (83.05%) | 254 (16.95%) |

We also instructed the Claude model to extract PII tokens using the identical procedure outlined in the manuscript. The results indicate that **most PII tokens identified by GPT-4o are also recovered by the Claude model**, demonstrating strong consistency between the two systems:

|  | Medical | Financial |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Percentage of intersection PII tokens | $85.10$% | $90.10$% |

[1] Hu et al. Knowledge-centric Hallucination Detection. EMNLP 2024.

[2] Stabb et al. Large Language Models are Advanced Anonymizers. ICLR 2025.

> W2. The datasets are synthetically generated using GPT-4o, and may not be reflective of real data. While the authors mention that they engaged domain experts to check the data, it would be good to give more details on what percentage of the documents were checked, and the methodology for checking.
>
>Q1. Could more details be given on how the datasets are checked to be similar to real data?
 

For the financial domain, all documents were reviewed by professionals currently working in the industry with 32 years of experience. Over the course of one week, they examined whether the entity distributions, record formats, terminology, and information flow were consistent with authentic financial documents. They compared our generated samples against real materials used in practice and provided feedback that led us to refine templates such as naming conventions and field types. The experts also noted that our dataset follows a U.S.‑style information‑system structure, and we have added guidance in Appendix B on adapting it to other regions.

For the medical domain, expert medical knowledge is grounded in the gold references from the ChatDoctor Healthcare dataset. In addition, a hospital director with 24 years of clinical experience was asked to review a set of patient records matching the number of documents in the financial domain, verifying that they resemble real clinical documentation and that the scenarios remain realistic within standard medical practice.

Together, these expert evaluations ensure that our synthetically generated datasets closely reflect the structure and content of real‑world financial and medical materials.

> W3. The main evaluation was only done on two LLMs. It might be useful to evaluate on a more diverse range of LLMs with different sizes to check that the results generalize.
> 

Thank you for the helpful suggestion. We are currently extending our evaluation to include a more diverse set of LLMs with varying sizes. Once the experiments are completed, we plan to incorporate the findings into a future version of the manuscript.

> W4. PEARL might lead to a higher computational cost and latency. 
>
>Q2. What is the computational overhead and latency of using PEARL?
 

We acknowledge that PEARL introduces additional computational cost and inference latency. Our primary goal in this initial work, however, was to establish a clear and extensible framework for entropy‑aware private decoding. We believe there is substantial room for future optimization—such as model‑specific tuning, approximation methods, or more efficient sampling strategies—to reduce overhead while preserving privacy guarantees.

To clarify the practical cost, the table below reports the average speed of each stage in our pipeline, measured on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU:

|  | Ensemble Generation (1st stage) | GPT Refil (2nd stage) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LLaMA 3.1 8B| $20.14$ tokens/s | $1.45$ seconds |
| Qwen 2.5 7B | $20.98$ tokens/s | $1.39$ seconds |

The majority of PEARL’s added latency comes from the second‑stage GPT Refill, which takes about 1.4–1.5 seconds per sample. Since the first stage runs at normal generation speed, the overall overhead remains moderate and can be further reduced through batching or parallelization within typical RAG pipelines.

summary.value:
This paper tackles the challenge of applying Differential Privacy (DP) to Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models, arguing that the standard privacy-utility trade-off overlooks the critical impact of DP on trustworthiness. The authors posit that DP-injected noise exacerbates hallucinations. The paper's core contribution is identifying the Confidence Gap (CG)---the entropy difference between a base model and a context-retrieval model---as a unified signal for two distinct risks. The key insight is that this signal is bimodal: low CG indicates high knowledge conflict and correlates with hallucinations, while high CG indicates regurgitation of context and correlates with PII leakage.
Based on this, the authors propose PEARL, a multi-stage private decoding framework. PEARL first generates an initial response using a standard DP mechanism. It then privately filters this response at the sentence level using CG to identify hallucination-prone spans ($S_U$) and PII-bearing spans ($S_P$). Finally, it reallocates the remaining privacy budget to redact the PII spans ($S_P$) while selectively regenerating the hallucination-prone spans ($S_U$) using a private refilling technique. Experiments on LeakRAG, two new RAG benchmarks (medical and financial) with explicit PII annotations created by the authors, demonstrate that PEARL simultaneously reduces hallucination scores and PII leakage compared to baselines.

strengths.value: S1. The paper's primary strength is its novel and important problem formulation. By shifting the focus from a simple "privacy-utility" trade-off to a more nuanced "privacy-trustworthiness" (i.e., hallucination) analysis, it addresses a key gap in prior work.

weaknesses.value:
W1. The experimental baselines are too simple and self-referential. The paper's main comparisons are against 'NOREFILL' and 'RANDOMFILL', which are ablations of the PEARL method itself, not external competitors. The related work section (Section 6) explicitly mentions other 'non-uniform privacy-budget allocation' methods (e.g., Wang et al., 2025), which are the true state-of-the-art. By omitting a comparison to these, the paper fails to demonstrate its superiority over existing, published work.

W2. The paper's definition of privacy risk is confusing due to a mismatch between its formal guarantee and its practical evaluation. The formal guarantee is document-level DP (Section 2.1), protecting against the influence of adding/removing one document. However, the evaluation (Section 5.3) uses a specific, fine-grained PII-extraction attack. This leaves the actual attack model and the practical privacy risk being addressed unclear. For instance, is the goal to protect the presence of a document (as DP implies) or to prevent the leakage of specific PII tokens (as the evaluation implies)? A model could satisfy the former but fail the latter (e.g., if PII appears in multiple documents), making it unclear what the DP guarantee actually achieves.

W3. The paper's framing of its insights can be an overclaim. The core observation that low CG correlates with hallucinations is a finding from prior work (which the paper cites as Bi et al. (2025)), making the experiment in Section 3.2 appear to be a replication of this previous finding that doesn't bring new insight, rather than a new discovery of this paper.

W4. The introduction of the new LeakRAG benchmark is presented as a major contribution, but it is not sufficiently motivated or elaborated. The paper does not situate this new benchmark within the existing literature on privacy or RAG benchmarks. Furthermore, the soundness of the new evaluation metrics (HalluScore, GoldAlign) and the precise definition of 'privacy' (which appears to be a specific list of PII types) are not well-explained or justified. Given this, presenting it as a significant benchmark seems overstated; it functions more as a new test dataset for this specific paper.

W5. The proposed PEARL framework (Algorithm 1) is a complex, multi-stage pipeline. A major confounding factor is that the refilling stage (Line 27) uses the OpenAI GPT-4o API as the "filling model", while the target LLMs being evaluated are LLaMa 3.1 8B and Qwen 2.5 7B. This introduces a massive, external, and significantly more powerful model into the loop. It is unclear how much of the performance gain (especially in reduced hallucination) is attributable to the PEARL framework versus simply getting a "second pass" from GPT-4o. The paper lacks a crucial ablation study using the same base model (e.g., LLaMa 8B) for both initial generation and refilling.

W6. The entire framework's success hinges on the Confidence Gap (CG) being a perfectly reliable and non-overlapping signal for PII and hallucinations. The paper shows a correlation (Figure 3) but does not stress-test this assumption. What happens if a sentence contains both a PII token and a hallucination? The framework's filtering (TOP-K or SVT) seems to assume these sets ($S_P$ and $S_U$) are disjoint. This potential "signal conflict" is not analyzed, and the model's behavior in this scenario is undefined.

questions.value: Q1. The epsilon = 0 baseline is labeled 'Zero-shot' in Table 1. This is confusing, as $\epsilon=0$ implies perfect privacy and infinite noise, which should result in random, useless output. However, the 'Zero-shot' model has high utility scores.

comment.value:
We sincerely appreciate the constructive and insightful comments from the reviewer. Here are our responses to the comments.

> W1. The experimental baselines are too simple and self-referential. The paper's main comparisons are against 'NOREFILL' and 'RANDOMFILL', which are ablations of the PEARL method itself, not external competitors. The related work section (Section 6) explicitly mentions other 'non-uniform privacy-budget allocation' methods (e.g., Wang et al., 2025), which are the true state-of-the-art. By omitting a comparison to these, the paper fails to demonstrate its superiority over existing, published work.
> 

We respectfully clarify that, to the best of our knowledge, **no prior work has investigated the relationship between differential privacy mechanisms and hallucination behavior in LLMs**. As a result, there is **no established state-of-the-art method** directly applicable to our task setting.

The work cited in Section 6 (Wang et al., 2025) is referenced **solely because it varies the privacy budget across steps**, not because it represents an SOTA baseline for hallucination mitigation. Their method is neither designed for hallucination reduction nor directly comparable to our setting.

Finally, the objective of our paper is **not to outperform all DP algorithms on a generic benchmark, but rather to introduce a new research direction that illuminates the trade-off between privacy and hallucination in LLMs**. Because no suitable benchmark for this phenomenon existed, we designed one from scratch to enable a clean and controlled analysis. Our baselines are therefore structured to isolate and examine this specific effect, not to claim superiority over unrelated privacy literature.

> W2. The paper's definition of privacy risk is confusing due to a mismatch between its formal guarantee and its practical evaluation. The formal guarantee is document-level DP (Section 2.1), protecting against the influence of adding/removing one document. However, the evaluation (Section 5.3) uses a specific, fine-grained PII-extraction attack. This leaves the actual attack model and the practical privacy risk being addressed unclear. For instance, is the goal to protect the presence of a document (as DP implies) or to prevent the leakage of specific PII tokens (as the evaluation implies)? A model could satisfy the former but fail the latter (e.g., if PII appears in multiple documents), making it unclear what the DP guarantee actually achieves.
> 

Our framework provides **document-level differential privacy. For the cases where an individual’s PII is distributed across multiple documents as the reviewer have pointed out**, the guarantee naturally extends to **group differential privacy**. If the same person’s PII appears in $k$ documents, the document-level DP guarantee scales to $(k\epsilon,\, k e^{(k-1)\epsilon}\delta)$-DP for groups of size $k$, meaning that the document-level privacy limits the leakage of individual PII instances, regardless of whether they appear in one or several documents.

**Therefore, the practical implication of this guarantee is straightforward:** it prevents the model from memorizing and leaking the PII contained in any individual document. This is precisely why our evaluation centers on a PII‑extraction attack—retrieving PII tokens is the most direct way to test whether the model has retained document-specific information that document-level DP is intended to suppress.

> W3. The paper's framing of its insights can be an overclaim. The core observation that low CG correlates with hallucinations is a finding from prior work (which the paper cites as Bi et al. (2025)), making the experiment in Section 3.2 appear to be a replication of this previous finding that doesn't bring new insight, rather than a new discovery of this paper.
> 

Section 3.2 includes not only the correlation between CG values and hallucination, but also the correlation between high CG values and PII leakage, which becomes accessible through our crafted benchmark. In addition, the work of Bi et al. focuses on the balance between parametric and contextual knowledge, **rather than systematically analyzing the correlation** **between CG values and hallucination** in a direct manner as we do. Finally, **we are the first to provide an analysis of how the confidence gap relates to hallucination amplification** in the context of private decoding, as presented in Proposition 1.

> W4. The introduction of the new LeakRAG benchmark is presented as a major contribution, but it is not sufficiently motivated or elaborated. The paper does not situate this new benchmark within the existing literature on privacy or RAG benchmarks. Furthermore, the soundness of the new evaluation metrics (HalluScore, GoldAlign) and the precise definition of 'privacy' (which appears to be a specific list of PII types) are not well-explained or justified. Given this, presenting it as a significant benchmark seems overstated; it functions more as a new test dataset for this specific paper.
> 

To clearly motivate our benchmark, we note that, to the best of our knowledge, there exist benchmarks in various domains [1,2,3]. However, there are no RAG benchmarks for evaluating privacy in the medical or financial domains **because the inclusion of real PIIs is legally restricted**. Furthermore, existing privacy benchmarks **lack structured documents that reflect real‑world application settings**. Therefore, we constructed a benchmark using synthesized PII, followed by expert validation. The scope of “privacy” in LeakRAG follows widely adopted data‑protection frameworks such as HIPAA and GDPR, focusing on personally identifiable information (PII) entities such as names, IDs, and contact details.

Lastly, The two metrics are not arbitrarily designed but build on **established GPT-based evaluation practices** that have become standard for measuring hallucination and answer consistency in recent literature (e.g., [4,5]). Our *HalluScore* follows the same paradigm to quantify semantic hallucination relative to supporting evidence, while *GoldAlign* measures alignment between predicted and reference privacy indicators. Their formulation aligns with prior validated approaches, so their soundness is consistent with the current evaluation methodology in the field. We describe detailed prompts in Section C.2.


> W5. “The proposed PEARL framework (Algorithm 1) is a complex, multi-stage pipeline.
A major confounding factor is that the refilling stage (Line 27) uses the OpenAI GPT-4o API
as the ‘filling model’, while the target LLMs being evaluated are LLaMa 3.1 8B and Qwen 2.5 7B.
This makes it unclear how much improvement is due to PEARL versus simply getting a second passfrom GPT-4o. The paper lacks an ablation using the same base model for both initial generation and refilling.”
> 

We understand the reviewer’s concern regarding the influence of the GPT model on the pipeline. 

Importantly, we chose GPT-4o **not to reduce hallucination through an external model, but because its strong instruction-following capability** is required for the controlled refill step—capabilities that the LLaMa 8B model does not reliably provide in our setting.

Thus, GPT-4o serves as a **mechanism to execute the refill instruction**, rather than as a source of additional knowledge or hallucination suppression.

To isolate the effect of GPT from the PEARL framework itself, we include an additional baseline, **Full Redaction**, which completely removes both parts $S_u$ and $S_p$ instead of refilling them with GPT. The corresponding performance for $\epsilon = 3, 6, 8$ is presented below. 

**ε = 3.0**

| Method | HalluScore $\downarrow$ | GoldAlign $\uparrow$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No Filling (Baseline) | 2.52 (±0.06) | 2.53 (±0.05) |
| Full Redaction (filtering) | 2.06 (±0.05) | 2.88 (±0.06) |
| Refill with GPT | **1.87 (±0.05)** | **3.06 (±0.03)** |

---

**ε = 6.0**

| Method | HalluScore $\downarrow$ | GoldAlign $\uparrow$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No Filling (Baseline) | 2.19 (±0.05) | 2.80 (±0.06) |
| Full Redaction (filtering) | 1.92 (±0.04) | 2.91 (±0.05) |
| Refill with GPT | **1.90 (±0.05)** | **3.08 (±0.04)** |

---

**ε = 8.0**

| Method | HalluScore $\downarrow$ | GoldAlign $\uparrow$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No Filling (Baseline) | 2.15 (±0.05) | 2.88 (±0.03) |
| Full Redaction (filtering) | 1.98 (±0.04) | 2.96 (±0.04) |
| Refill with GPT | **1.87 (±0.04)** | **3.14 (±0.02)** |

From these results, we observe that **Full Redaction** **also improves faithfulness compared** to the *No Filling* baseline. However, its GoldAlign score is lower than that of the refill model, likely due to the unnaturally fragmented text flow resulting from removing segments without refilling them. These results support that the PEARL framework—not the GPT model—drives the hallucination reduction, while GPT’s role is limited to maintaining natural text flow after redaction. It indicates that any filler model can effectively reduce the hallucination of the LLM responses.

Thanks for the detailed rebuttal. My concerns regarding W3, W5, and W6 have been addressed. However, the following issues remain, as listed below. I also kindly remind the authors that the **PDF may be revised** during the discussion period.

**W1.** Targeting hallucination does not automatically imply strong hallucination-reduction performance. Even if prior work did not explicitly aim at hallucination mitigation, methods that allocate privacy budgets non-uniformly or adopt alternative DP decoding strategies remain the closest state-of-the-art comparators for privacy/utility/leakage. A comparison against such baselines is therefore still necessary.

**W2.** The rebuttal’s explanation that document-level DP extends to group-DP when PII spans multiple documents seems reasonable. However, this claim should be formally stated and proved. In addition, the threat model should be clarified and aligned more precisely with the practical privacy risk evaluated in the paper.

**W4.** While the motivation is plausible, the claimed advantages of LeakRAG over existing literature are still unconvincing, and several assertions require substantially more support. For example, the statement that “there are no RAG benchmarks for evaluating privacy in the medical or financial domains because the inclusion of real PIIs is legally restricted” is too vague without specifying: (1) what scope of RAG benchmarks is being considered, (2) which aspect(s) of privacy are benchmarked, (3) what types of RAG systems are targeted, (4) what unique challenges arise in medical and financial settings, and (5) how LeakRAG differs from or improves upon existing benchmarks [2,4] and datasets used in prior papers [1,3,5]. If LeakRAG is presented as a major benchmark contribution, much more effort is needed to clarify and justify these points.

**Q1.** I understand that $\epsilon = 0$ yields the worst performance, but the experimental meaning and implementation of the “zero-shot” $\epsilon = 0$ setting remain unclear. A clear definition of this baseline and how $\epsilon = 0$ is realized in code is important but currently missing.

> **W2.** The rebuttal’s explanation that document-level DP extends to group-DP when PII spans multiple documents seems reasonable. However, this claim should be formally stated and proved. In addition, **the threat model should be clarified and aligned more precisely with the practical privacy risk evaluated in the paper.**
> 

### **Privacy implication**

Our differential privacy (DP) framework adopts **document-level privacy**, meaning that the model’s output is designed to remain largely unchanged with or without the inclusion of **a single document associated with a specific user**. This aligns with practical privacy guarantees for applications involving retrieval-augmented generation systems over user-level data.  In the RAG setting, where documents correspond to user records or notes, this captures the practical requirement that the system’s responses should not reveal whether any particular user document is present in the retrieval corpus.

By standard **group privacy** [3], this guarantee naturally extends to users whose PII spans multiple documents.

**Group Privacy [3]**

If a mechanism $M$ is ($\varepsilon, \delta$)-differentially private (DP), and two datasets $x$, $x'$ differ in at most $k$ entries, then group privacy guarantees that

$$
\Pr[M(x) \in S] \le e^{k\varepsilon} \Pr[M(x') \in S] + k e^{k\varepsilon} \delta.
$$

We have included the **proof of group privacy in the** **Appendix B of the revised manuscript.** For the case a single user may contribute up to $k$ documents,  if our mechanism is $(\varepsilon, \delta)$-DP at the document level, then by group privacy it is $(k\varepsilon, k e^{k\varepsilon}\delta)$-DP at the user level.

### **Threat model**

We assume a **black-box** setting: a malicious attacker has **no access to the internal state or parameters** of the LLM, and can only interact with the system by submitting queries and observing the outputs.

The attacker knows that the model is assisted by **in-context examples / retrieved documents** that may contain **private user information**, but does not know the exact content of those documents. The attacker can issue arbitrary (possibly adaptive) queries, including prompts such as:

> “Provide a similar case and include the actual personal information (e.g., name, address, phone number).”
> 

The attacker’s goal is to **extract PII about a specific user** whose data may appear in the in-context samples or retrieved documents.

Our DP framework is designed to limit **how much the model’s output distribution — including outputs that contain PII attributes (e.g., age) can change** when a single user’s document is added or removed. Concretely, by enforcing **document-level (ε, δ)-DP** over the private corpus, we ensure that the model’s output distribution does not change significantly when a single user’s document is added or removed. By group privacy, this guarantee naturally extends to PII that may be spread across multiple documents belonging to the same user.

### **Why we focus on PII‑leakage attacks instead of membership attacks**

While document‑level membership inference aligns more directly with the *formal* DP definition, we evaluate **PII‑leakage attacks** because:

1. **They match real‑world harm.**
In practice (e.g., under GDPR/HIPAA), the primary concern is whether the system reveals **concrete identifiers** (name, address, phone, ID, etc.), not just whether a particular document was in the training or retrieval set.
2. **They better fit RAG usage.**
In RAG, many documents are semantically similar or overlapping, so “document membership” is often hard to interpret. In contrast, PII‑leakage directly tests whether an attacker can extract **sensitive user attributes**, which is a clearer and more actionable notion of privacy failure.

Note that any PII‑leakage attack can be viewed as a **particular form of membership (or attribute) inference attack**, since the adversary uses the model’s outputs to infer whether specific sensitive attributes about a user are present in the underlying corpus. Our PII‑extraction experiments should therefore be viewed as an **empirical validation of the DP framework in a realistic RAG setting**, rather than as a separate privacy notion.

> **W4.** While the motivation is plausible, the claimed advantages of LeakRAG over existing literature are still unconvincing, and several assertions require substantially more support. ... If LeakRAG is presented as a major benchmark contribution, much more effort is needed to clarify and justify these points.
>

### **Scope of RAG benchmarks being considered**

In our paper, we specifically consider **retrieval-augmented generation benchmarks that couple a retriever with a generator over a fixed document corpus**, and that evaluate end-to-end performance on document-grounded tasks. Prior benchmarks and datasets [2–5] fall into this category: they assess general RAG utility, explainability, or domain-specific QA (e.g., medical or financial question answering) but, to the best of our knowledge, **none are specifically designed to evaluate privacy-leakage behavior** induced by the retrieval–generation pipeline over structured domain documents.

### **Which aspects of privacy are benchmarked?**

Existing work related to privacy in RAG either (a) **avoids PII entirely** in the evaluation corpora, or (b) studies **high-level privacy risks** such as the use of synthetic data to mitigate potential leakage [1], without providing a task benchmark. In contrast, LeakRAG explicitly benchmarks **fine-grained, entity-level privacy leakage**: we test whether a RAG system’s responses expose sensitive PII entities (e.g., names, contact details, identifiers) that are present in the underlying documents or hallucinated by the model. Thus, the benchmark is aligned with **practical PII-exfiltration risks**, rather than only abstract membership inference.

### **Targeted RAG system**

LeakRAG is designed for **safety-critical RAG systems** that retrieve from **structured medical or financial documents** (e.g., clinical notes, financial counseling logs) and generate natural-language responses for end users. These systems operate under strict compliance constraints where real PIIs must not be surfaced, yet still need to provide faithful, document-grounded answers. This setting differs from prior general-purpose RAG benchmarks [2] and domain QA datasets [3,4], which mainly target accuracy, explainability, or general utility, and **do not evaluate whether the RAG pipeline leaks PII.**

### **What challenges arise in medical and financial domains?**

Medical and financial domains present **unique privacy and modeling challenges**:

(1) Documents contain **highly sensitive PII** (names, addresses, policy IDs, account numbers, etc.) tightly interwoven with task-relevant content.

(2) Strong regulatory regimes such as **HIPAA and GDPR** impose legal restrictions on storing and sharing real PII, which makes it **infeasible to release public benchmarks** with genuine identifiers.

(3) The documents are often **long and structured** (sections, templates, tabular content), which interacts non-trivially with retrieval and generation.

To address these challenges, LeakRAG uses **expert-validated synthetic PII** that preserves realistic document structure and entity patterns, enabling controlled privacy evaluation in settings where real PII cannot be used.

### **How LeakRAG differs from or improves upon existing benchmarks**

LeakRAG is complementary to, and distinct from, existing work in several ways:

- **RAGBench [2]**: focuses on explainability and faithfulness of RAG (e.g., how well answers align with retrieved evidence), but **does not evaluate privacy leakage or PII exposure**.
- **Medical RAG for fitness assessment [3]** and **quantitative finance RAG benchmarking [4]**: evaluate **task performance and accuracy** in domain QA, without measuring privacy leakage, hallucinated identifiers, or PII-specific risks.
- **Synthetic-data privacy work [1]**: proposes using synthetic data to mitigate privacy concerns, but **does not provide a retrieval-grounded benchmark** with structured documents and explicit PII-leakage tasks.
- **Federated RAG survey [5]**: offers a **systematic overview** of federated RAG approaches, but **does not release a benchmark dataset**.

In contrast, **LeakRAG provides a concrete, retrieval‑grounded benchmark with structured medical and financial documents, synthetic yet realistic PII**. To the best of our knowledge, this addresses an important gap not covered by [1–5]: a public benchmark for medical and financial RAG that combines structured documents with (synthetic) PII and explicit PII annotations for privacy‑focused evaluation. We will clarify these distinctions explicitly in the revised manuscript.

To make these distinctions explicit, we have included the comparison table in the Appendix of the revised manuscript.

comment.value:
I thank the authors for their detailed response and the revised manuscript. I particularly appreciate that the baseline comparison concern was addressed by integrating comparisons to other DP algorithms and clarifying that the proposed method is an orthogonal mechanism.

However, I still have reservations regarding the theoretical framing and the evaluation benchmarks presented in this study.

### **Theory and Adjacency Definition**
I have reviewed the updated definition and proof in Appendix B alongside the standard definition of Group Privacy (Vadhan, 2017). While the proof is mathematically consistent with the standard definition regarding database records, there remains a fundamental gap when translating "database rows" to "text documents" in the definition of **adjacency**.

The paper defines a group as "users whose data spans multiple documents." This definition relies on an implicit assumption: **that a document contributed by a specific user contains the PII of only that user.** This assumption is not explicitly stated in the paper or the response, yet it is critical for the privacy guarantee to hold. In a realistic RAG setting, this is rarely guaranteed; even personal documents (like diaries or clinical notes) frequently contain PII regarding third parties.

### **Evaluation and Benchmark Utility**
While I acknowledge the clarifications provided, I find it difficult to fully appreciate the contribution of the proposed benchmark for the following reasons:

* **Strong Assumption in Dataset Construction:** Similar to the theoretical concern raised above, the LeakRAG benchmark appears to be constructed under the same idealized assumption. By generating synthetic patient records or financial logs that strictly map to single individuals, the evaluation artificially enforces the "one document = one user" constraint. This design prevents the benchmark from testing the system’s robustness in realistic scenarios where documents contain mixed-ownership data or third-party PII—precisely the failure mode where the proposed privacy definition is most vulnerable.
* **Literature Comparison:** Although the authors included the specific papers I explicitly mentioned in the previous review, the comparison still lacks the comprehensive and systematic scope expected of a contribution that aims to establish a new benchmark.
* **Reliability of Hallucination Metrics:** The evaluation relies heavily on an LLM (GPT-4o) as a judge. Without robust mechanisms to mitigate or measure the evaluator's own hallucinations (e.g., ensemble evaluation, or uncertainty quantification), the metric may lack the reliability required for a benchmark intended to serve as a gold standard for future optimization of hallucination-mitigation algorithms.

### **Conclusion**
I recognize the value of this work in identifying the phenomenon that "DP may increase hallucination," which is a novel and interesting insight. Consequently, I have decided to increase my rating. However, due to the theoretical limitations regarding the adjacency assumption and the circularity in the evaluation design, I maintain a slightly negative score. I am not entirely opposed to the manuscript's acceptance, but I believe these gaps limit its current impact.

comment.value:
*We sincerely appreciate the effort of the reviewer thoroughly reading the response and reflecting the score! Nevertheless, we would like to address a few points that may have been misunderstood.*

### **About the meaning of “group” in the privacy**

We would like to clarify that in our paper, “group” in the group privacy argument **does not refer to a group of different users**. Instead, it refers to **the set of documents contributed by a single user,**.  We apologize if this meaning was not sufficiently clear in the manuscript.

### **About translating "database rows" to "text documents" in the definition of adjacency**

In differential privacy, the notion of **a “database row” is not tied to any fixed physical unit; it is a modeling choice** that specifies what counts as one individual’s contribution. In many applications, this contribution can be a complex structured object (e.g., a document, a session, or a trajectory), rather than a single scalar record.

In our setting, we intentionally define adjacency at the document level, treating each document as the protected unit. This is consistent with standard DP practice in text and IR applications where one individual contributes an entire document or record. Translating “rows” to “documents” therefore does not violate the DP definition; it reflects our chosen privacy granularity.

### **Privacy does not disappear in the multi-document case—it scales as expected**

Under group privacy, if a single user contributes up to $k$ documents, then a mechanism that is $\varepsilon$-DP at the document level becomes at most $k\varepsilon$-DP at the user level. This means that **the privacy guarantee does not collapse entirely**, even when a user’s data spans multiple documents; instead, the guarantee weakens in a mathematically controlled and well-understood manner. 

### **About reflecting the realistic RAG setting**

We acknowledge that real-world documents (e.g., diaries, clinical notes) may include incidental third-party mentions. However, **many practical RAG deployments in medical, financial, and enterprise environments organize corpora explicitly by user or account**, making a document-level unit a realistic modeling choice. For example:

- **Clinical notes in EMR/EHR systems** are indexed by patient identifier and primarily describe that patient’s history and treatment.
- **Bank statements** summarize transactions for a single account holder over a given period.
- **Customer support tickets** are keyed to a single customer or case ID and record one user’s inquiry or issue.

In these settings, treating a document (or a tightly related set of documents) as one user’s contribution is standard for storage, retrieval, and compliance. Our “one document ↔ one user” assumption aims to capture this common regime, and domain experts involved in LeakRAG confirmed that it reflects a substantial share of real workflows.

**We acknowledge that more complex scenarios with mixed-ownership documents are also important and represent an interesting extension.** Our setup can naturally accommodate “one user–multiple documents” settings by grouping paraphrased or related documents under the same user ID, without changing the core methodology of our evaluation. 

### **About the reliability of hallucination metrics**

We acknowledge the concern that an LLM judge can itself hallucinate. We performed two types of checks to assess robustness:

- **Cross-model agreement.** We re-annotated hallucinations using another strong LLM (Claude Sonnet 4.5) under the same protocol. In the medical domain, GPT-4o and Claude agreed on 3,164 / 3,330 cases (95.64%), and in the financial domain, on 1,245 / 1,499 cases (83.05%). The qualitative trends across different $\varepsilon$ settings were consistent across the two judges.
- **Expert review.** Medical domain experts reviewed a randomly sampled 10% subset of the medical cases. They did not identify hallucinations in this subset and judged the outputs to be consistent with academically standard statements for a tertiary hospital setting.

These checks suggest that, while not perfect, the labels are **sufficiently stable for the relative comparisons** that our paper focuses on (e.g., how hallucination and PII-leakage rates change as $\varepsilon$ varies). We will include these agreement statistics and a clearer discussion of their limitations in the revised version.

At the same time, **we agree that developing** **more reliable hallucination metrics** **is an important direction**. In future extensions of LeakRAG, we plan to incorporate (i) ensemble-based judging across multiple LLMs, and (ii) uncertainty or disagreement signals as part of the benchmark’s official metrics.

summary.value: This paper introduces PEARL, a novel framework for differentially private and entropy-aware regulated language generation in LLMs, specifically addressing the trade-off between factual accuracy (from Retrieval-Augmented Generation - RAG) and privacy. The authors identify that Differential Privacy (DP) mechanisms, while protecting sensitive information, can inadvertently increase "hallucination" (generation of non-factual content) in LLM outputs.

strengths.value:
S1. The concept of using a "confidence gap" (CG) to guide privacy budget allocation and mitigate hallucination in DP settings is novel and well-motivated.

S2. The authors clearly articulate how DP noise can exacerbate knowledge conflicts and hallucination, laying a strong foundation for their proposed PEARL framework.

S3. new, scenario-grounded RAG benchmarks with explicit PII annotations in medical and financial domains is a significant contribution.

S4. Strong experimental results and evaluation (BERTScore, GoldAlign, and HalluScore provide a multi-faceted evaluation of the model's performance). PEARL consistenly outperforms existing baselines.

weaknesses.value:
W1. A more intuitive explanation of CG or a small illustrative example in Section 2.2 could enhance understanding for readers less familiar with entropy differences in this context.

W2. While PEARL aims to mitigate the computational cost of considering privacy and hallucination at every decoding token, a more explicit discussion or quantification of PEARL's computational overhead compared to simpler DP decoding methods would be beneficial.

W3. The privacy attack involves appending a "malicious instruction." While this is a good stress test, a brief discussion on how typical prompt engineering strategies (without malicious intent) might influence PII leakage in baseline models versus PEARL could add more context.

W5. Figure 1 Description: The text "privacy-related knowledge should not be factually disclosed, while general knowledge may be affected by DP-induced hallucination" is helpful, but consider adding a brief statement directly describing the visual elements of the diagram itself, beyond just the concept.
